title: First Flight
status: DRAFT — for review by an English teacher before any question is approved
source: Written against NCERT Class X English 'First Flight' (jeff1, reprint 2026-27), read from the chapter PDFs, to the CBSE English Language and Literature (184) question paper design for 2025-26. Extracts are quoted from the book and checked word for word by scripts/check-english-questions.mjs.

questions.stem: In his second letter, Lencho calls the post-office employees 'a bunch of crooks'. What makes this situation ironic?

options.text: The postmaster had kept the rest of the money for himself.
The employees were the very people who had collected money to help him.
Lencho had never actually received any money.
The first letter had not been posted at all.

questions.explanation: The postmaster, his employees and friends gave their own money so that Lencho's faith would not be shaken. Lencho accuses exactly these people of stealing — the opposite of what really happened, which is what makes it ironic.

questions.stem: 'Lencho was an ox of a man, working like an animal in the fields.' Which quality of an ox does this metaphor transfer to Lencho?

options.text: Stubbornness in an argument
Slowness in understanding
Strength and the capacity for hard physical work
Gentleness towards other animals

questions.explanation: The sentence itself explains the comparison: Lencho worked 'like an animal in the fields'. An ox is valued for its strength and for heavy labour, and that quality is transferred to Lencho.

questions.stem: In 'Fire and Ice', the poet says that for destruction ice 'is also great / And would suffice'. Reading the poem closely, what does ice most likely stand for?

options.text: Desire
Greed
Hope
Hatred

questions.explanation: The poet links fire to 'desire' ('From what I've tasted of desire / I hold with those who favour fire') and ice to 'hate' ('I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great'). Ice stands for hatred — cold, rigid and indifferent.

questions.stem: In 'The postmaster -- a fat, amiable fellow -- also broke out laughing', the relative pronoun and verb are 'hidden', as in the story's first sentence. Which rewriting shows them correctly?

options.text: The postmaster -- which was a fat, amiable fellow -- also broke out laughing.
The postmaster -- who was a fat, amiable fellow -- also broke out laughing.
The postmaster -- whose was a fat, amiable fellow -- also broke out laughing.
The postmaster -- whom was a fat, amiable fellow -- also broke out laughing.

questions.explanation: The chapter shows that 'the only one in the entire valley' hides 'which was'. Here the phrase describes a person who is the subject of the clause, so the hidden words are 'who was'. 'Which' is for things, 'whose' shows possession and 'whom' is an object form.

questions.stem: The boys 'ran out to collect the frozen pearls'. What quality of pearls does this metaphor transfer to the hailstones?

options.text: Their high price in the market
The fact that they come from the sea
Their habit of melting quickly in the hand
Their small, round, white and shining look

questions.explanation: The hailstones are small balls of ice, white and gleaming, so they look like pearls; 'frozen' tells us what they really are. The sentence before says they 'truly did resemble new silver coins' — the boys see them as something bright and precious, before the hail destroys the crop.

questions.extract: Lencho showed not the slightest surprise on seeing the money; such was his confidence -- but he became angry when he counted the money. God could not have made a mistake, nor could he have denied Lencho what he had requested. Immediately, Lencho went up to the window to ask for paper and ink. On the public writing-table, he started to write, with much wrinkling of his brow, caused by the effort he had to make to express his ideas.

parts.prompt: Lencho 'showed not the slightest surprise' on seeing the money because he

options.text: was confident that God would answer his letter
had already been told that money had come
expected the postmaster to help him
did not really need the money

parts.answer: (a) — 'such was his confidence': he was certain God would answer.

parts.prompt: Which phrase in the extract shows that writing did not come easily to Lencho?
parts.answer: 'with much wrinkling of his brow' (caused by the effort he had to make to express his ideas).

parts.prompt: The word 'denied', as used in the extract, means

options.text: delayed
refused to give
forgotten
doubled

parts.answer: (b) refused to give.

parts.prompt: Why did Lencho become angry when he counted the money? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He found only seventy of the hundred pesos he had asked for. Since he believed God could neither make a mistake nor refuse him, he concluded that someone at the post office had taken the rest. (1 mark: the shortfall; 1 mark: why he blamed the post office.)

questions.extract:
The way a crow
Shook down on me
The dust of snow
From a hemlock tree

Has given my heart
A change of mood
And saved some part
Of a day I had rued.

parts.prompt: A crow and a hemlock tree are usually associated with

options.text: love and friendship
wealth and success
gloom and sorrow
joy and celebration

parts.answer: (c) gloom and sorrow — a crow is seen as a bad omen and the hemlock is a poisonous tree, which makes the lift in the poet's mood the more surprising.

parts.prompt: What does the word 'rued' mean?
parts.answer: Held in regret; regretted.

parts.prompt: The poet's mood changes because

options.text: the snow stops falling
he climbs a hemlock tree
the sun comes out after the snow
a crow shakes snow down on him from a tree

parts.answer: (d) a crow shakes the dust of snow down on him from a hemlock tree.

parts.prompt: How can a small moment 'save some part' of a bad day? Answer in 30–40 words with reference to the poem.
parts.answer: A small, unexpected event can break a gloomy mood. The poet's day was one he 'had rued', but the dust of snow from the crow cheered him, so the rest of the day was not wasted. (1 mark: the change of mood; 1 mark: link to the poem.)

questions.extract: But in the hearts of all who lived in that solitary house in the middle of the valley, there was a single hope: help from God. "Don't be so upset, even though this seems like a total loss. Remember, no one dies of hunger." "That's what they say: no one dies of hunger." All through the night, Lencho thought only of his one hope: the help of God, whose eyes, as he had been instructed, see everything, even what is deep in one's conscience.

parts.prompt: The 'single hope' of the family after the hailstorm was

options.text: that the hail would stop quickly
that some of the corn could still be sold
help from God
help from their neighbours in the valley

parts.answer: (c) help from God — 'there was a single hope: help from God.' (The house was the only one in the valley, so there were no neighbours to turn to.)

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract means 'an inner sense of right and wrong'?
parts.answer: Conscience.

parts.prompt: The reply 'That's what they say: no one dies of hunger' most probably shows that the speaker

options.text: repeats a common saying for comfort, without being fully sure of it
knows that food will soon arrive from the town
is angry at being told not to be upset
believes the corn will grow again by itself

parts.answer: (a) — 'That's what they say' turns the comfort into a saying other people repeat, which suggests the speaker wants to believe it but is not certain.

parts.prompt: What does 'whose eyes, as he had been instructed, see everything' tell us about Lencho's faith? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Lencho had been taught that God sees everything, even what is deep in one's conscience. He believed this completely, so he was sure God knew of his trouble and would help — which led him to write a letter to God. (1 mark: what he had been taught; 1 mark: how firmly he believed it / what it led him to do.)

questions.extract:
Some say the world will end in fire
Some say in ice.
From what I've tasted of desire
I hold with those who favour fire.

But if it had to perish twice,
I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice.

parts.prompt: The poet opens the poem by

options.text: describing a fire he once saw
warning that the world will end very soon
presenting two views people hold about how the world will end
explaining the science of heat and cold

parts.answer: (c) — 'Some say the world will end in fire / Some say in ice.'

parts.prompt: Which phrase shows that the poet speaks from his own experience of desire?
parts.answer: 'From what I've tasted of desire'.

parts.prompt: 'I hold with those who favour fire' means that the poet

options.text: agrees with those who believe the world will end in fire
prefers warm weather to cold weather
wants to set the world on fire
holds a burning torch with other people

parts.answer: (a) he agrees with those who believe the world will end in fire.

parts.prompt: The poem speaks of the end of the world in calm, simple words and ends with the short lines 'Is also great / And would suffice'. What effect does this quiet tone have? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The calm, almost casual tone makes the idea more chilling: the poet treats destruction as a plain fact. The short final lines fall quietly, the way hatred destroys coldly and without noise. Accept other well-argued readings. (1 mark: the effect of the understatement; 1 mark: link to the closing lines.)

questions.extract:
But if it had to perish twice,
I think I know enough of hate
To say that for destruction ice
Is also great
And would suffice.

parts.prompt: In 'But if it had to perish twice', the word 'it' refers to

options.text: the fire
the ice
hate
the world

parts.answer: (d) the world — the poem opens 'Some say the world will end in fire'.

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract means 'be sufficient'?
parts.answer: Suffice.

parts.prompt: The poet feels able to judge the destructive power of ice because he

options.text: has lived through many cold winters
knows enough of hate
has studied how the world was formed
has already seen the world perish once

parts.answer: (b) he knows enough of hate — 'I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great'.

parts.prompt: Why does the poet imagine the world having 'to perish twice', and what does this suggest about human nature? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He imagines that even if fire (desire) destroyed the world once, ice (hate) would be strong enough to destroy it again. This suggests both destructive forces — desire and hatred — are present in people, and either alone is enough. (1 mark: the two destructions; 1 mark: what it says about human nature.)

questions.stem: Why did the postmaster decide to answer Lencho's letter, and why did he sign the reply 'God'? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: He was moved by Lencho's faith: 'What faith! I wish I had the faith of the man who wrote this letter.'
He did not want to shake the writer's faith in God.
He collected money from his employees and friends and gave part of his own salary.
He signed it 'God' so that Lencho would believe God himself had answered.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Why he answered (faith, not wanting to shake it) and why he signed it 'God'. Any two of the value points, correctly linked.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: How did the rain first raise Lencho's hopes, and how were those hopes destroyed? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: His field of ripe corn needed only a downpour or a shower.
When big drops fell he called them 'new coins' — ten cent pieces and fives — promising a good harvest.
A strong wind brought very large hailstones that fell for an hour.
The field was white 'as if covered with salt'; the corn was totally destroyed.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The hope the rain brought (the 'new coins') and the hailstorm that destroyed the crop.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: 'A Letter to God' shows a conflict between humans and nature, and a conflict between humans themselves. Give one example of each. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Humans and nature: the hailstorm destroys the crop Lencho has worked for, leaving his family facing hunger.
Humans themselves: Lencho distrusts the post-office employees and calls them 'a bunch of crooks'.
The second conflict exists only in Lencho's mind — the employees had in fact helped him.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: One correct example of each conflict (1 mark each).

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: In 'Fire and Ice', what do 'fire' and 'ice' stand for, and why does the poet believe either could end the world? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Fire stands for desire — greed, lust, fury — which burns and spreads quickly.
Ice stands for hatred — coldness, rigidity, indifference — which destroys slowly.
The poet has 'tasted of desire' and knows 'enough of hate', so he judges either is powerful enough to destroy the world.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: What fire and ice symbolise, and the poet's reason that either would suffice.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Would you describe Lencho as 'naive' and 'unquestioning'? Support your view with evidence from the story. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: He writes a letter addressed 'To God' and posts it, believing God will send money by post.
He shows 'not the slightest surprise' on seeing the money — such was his confidence.
He never asks who really sent the money.
He is sure God cannot make a mistake, so he blames the post-office employees without any proof.
Accept a reasoned alternative view (e.g. deep, simple faith rather than foolishness) if supported by the text.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: A clear view on whether he is naive and unquestioning, supported by at least two details from the story.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: What is the rhyme scheme of 'Fire and Ice', and how does it help bring out the contrasting ideas in the poem? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: The rhyme scheme is abaabcbcb (fire / desire / fire; ice / twice / ice / suffice; hate / great).
The two main rhyme sounds are built on the two key words, 'fire' and 'ice'.
The 'fire' rhymes dominate the first part and the 'ice' rhymes the second, so the sounds move with the argument from desire to hate.
The interlocking pattern holds the two opposites together, suggesting both are equally possible ends.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: States the rhyme scheme correctly (1) and explains how the rhymes on 'fire' and 'ice' reflect the contrast (1).

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: The postmaster and his employees gave their own money to help a stranger whose letter they had first laughed at — and were then called crooks for it. Imagine you are the postmaster. Write a diary entry, in about 100–120 words, on the day you read Lencho's second letter: what you felt, and whether you still believe helping him was the right thing to do.
valuePoints: Written as a diary entry: date, first person, reflective tone.
Feelings on reading the letter — hurt, amusement or sadness at being called a crook.
Why he helped: Lencho's faith, and not wanting to shake it.
A considered answer on whether helping was right — for example, that kindness does not depend on thanks.
Some understanding of Lencho's position: poor, desperate, and unaware of who really sent the money.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Feelings, reasons for helping and a reasoned judgement, drawn from the story and going beyond it.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Diary format (date, first person); ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and tone.

questions.stem: Lencho lost his entire crop in one hour, yet his family said, 'no one dies of hunger', and he held on to hope. Write an article for your school magazine, in about 100–120 words, titled 'When Things Go Wrong: Faith, Hope and Effort'. Draw on Lencho's story, and suggest how a young person can respond to a setback they could not prevent.
valuePoints: Article format: title, and a clear opening that sets out the idea.
Lencho's situation: total loss, and the single hope that kept the family going.
Hope helps a person carry on, but it works best alongside effort and asking for help.
Practical ways a student can cope with a setback — talking to someone, planning the next step, not losing heart.
A reasoned conclusion.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Uses Lencho's story and extends it to real advice for coping with a setback.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Article format with a title; ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and tone.

questions.stem: Lencho counted seventy pesos instead of a hundred and at once decided that the post-office employees were 'a bunch of crooks' — when they were the very people who had helped him. Something goes missing from a classroom, and a few students immediately blame a classmate. Write a speech for the morning assembly, in about 100–120 words, titled 'Think Before You Blame', using Lencho's mistake to show why we should check the facts before accusing anyone.
valuePoints: Speech format: greeting the audience, stating the topic, a closing thank-you.
Lencho's hasty conclusion, and the irony that he accused the people who had helped him.
The harm a false accusation causes — hurt feelings, lost trust, a damaged reputation.
Practical steps: find out the facts, ask calmly, speak to a teacher, avoid spreading rumours.
A reasoned conclusion.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Uses Lencho's mistake and extends it to sensible ways of checking facts before blaming someone.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Speech format (address, opening, conclusion); ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and tone.

questions.stem: Mandela writes that 'the oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed'. Why does he believe the oppressor is not free either?

options.text: The oppressor lives in fear of being arrested by the new government.
The oppressor is 'a prisoner of hatred', locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness.
The oppressor has lost his land and wealth now that apartheid has ended.
The oppressor must obey laws made by the international leaders.

questions.explanation: Mandela says, 'A man who takes away another man's freedom is a prisoner of hatred; he is locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrowmindedness.' Hatred imprisons the oppressor's own mind, so 'the oppressed and the oppressor alike are robbed of their humanity.'

questions.stem: At the inauguration the highest generals saluted Mandela, though 'not so many years before they would not have saluted but arrested' him. What does their salute show most clearly?

options.text: The generals had been ordered by the visiting world leaders to salute him.
Mandela had once served as an officer in the defence force.
The army wished to display its ribbons and medals to the guests.
The military's loyalty now lay with a democracy and a freely elected government.

questions.explanation: Mandela calls the ceremony 'a demonstration of the military's loyalty to democracy, to a new government that had been freely and fairly elected'. The men who once would have arrested him now 'pledged their loyalty' — a sign of how completely power had changed hands.

questions.stem: In 'A Tiger in the Zoo', two stanzas begin 'He should be...'. What do these stanzas describe?

options.text: The life the tiger naturally belongs to, in the wild
The day the tiger was captured by hunters
What the visitors to the zoo imagine the tiger is thinking
The life the tiger will lead once the zoo sets him free

questions.explanation: 'Should' marks what ought to be but is not: the tiger 'should be lurking in shadow ... Near the water hole' and 'snarling around houses / At the jungle's edge'. The next stanza returns to the reality — 'But he's locked in a concrete cell'.

questions.stem: Mandela writes that oppression 'produced the Oliver Tambos, the Walter Sisulus ... of our time'. In which sentence is 'the' used with a name in the same way?

options.text: The Sharmas have moved into the house next door.
We visited the Taj Mahal during the holidays.
Our coach hopes to train the Mary Koms of tomorrow.
The Ganga flows past many old towns.

questions.explanation: In the text, 'the Oliver Tambos' means many people of the same kind as Oliver Tambo. 'The Mary Koms of tomorrow' likewise means people like Mary Kom. 'The Sharmas' means one family, and 'the Taj Mahal' and 'the Ganga' simply name one monument and one river.

questions.stem: 'Even in the grimmest times in prison ... I would see a glimmer of humanity in one of the guards, perhaps just for a second.' What does 'a glimmer of humanity' mean here?

options.text: A brief sign of human kindness in someone who was otherwise harsh
A ray of light shining into the prison cell
A guard who secretly joined the struggle against apartheid
A plan by the guards to set the prisoners free

questions.explanation: A glimmer is a faint, brief light, and 'perhaps just for a second' confirms it was momentary. What Mandela glimpsed was goodness, which 'was enough to reassure me and keep me going' — 'Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.'

questions.extract: It is from these comrades in the struggle that I learned the meaning of courage. Time and again, I have seen men and women risk and give their lives for an idea. I have seen men stand up to attacks and torture without breaking, showing a strength and resilience that defies the imagination. I learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.

parts.prompt: According to the extract, Mandela learned the meaning of courage from

options.text: the guards in his prison
the international leaders at the inauguration
his comrades in the struggle
his father and the customs of his tribe

parts.answer: (c) his comrades in the struggle — 'It is from these comrades in the struggle that I learned the meaning of courage.'

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract means 'the ability to deal with any kind of hardship and recover from its effects'?
parts.answer: Resilience.

parts.prompt: 'Courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.' This means that a brave person

options.text: feels fear but overcomes it
never feels afraid of anything
hides fear by pretending to others
stays away from situations that cause fear

parts.answer: (a) feels fear but overcomes it — 'The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers that fear.'

parts.prompt: Mandela believes that 'depths of oppression' can create 'heights of character'. How do his comrades illustrate this? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Decades of oppression and brutality produced men like Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu and Chief Luthuli, of extraordinary courage, wisdom and generosity. Such people risked and gave their lives for an idea and stood up to torture without breaking. (1 mark: oppression produced great character; 1 mark: an example of that courage.)

questions.extract:
But he's locked in a concrete cell,
His strength behind bars,
Stalking the length of his cage,
Ignoring visitors.

He hears the last voice at night,
The patrolling cars,
And stares with his brilliant eyes
At the brilliant stars.

parts.prompt: The 'concrete cell' in the extract is

options.text: the tiger's den in the jungle
a prison for criminals near the zoo
a house at the jungle's edge
the tiger's cage in the zoo

parts.answer: (d) the tiger's cage in the zoo.

parts.prompt: Which line of the extract suggests that the tiger's power is wasted?
parts.answer: 'His strength behind bars'.

parts.prompt: The tiger 'stares with his brilliant eyes / At the brilliant stars' most probably because he

options.text: is counting the stars to pass the night
longs for the freedom of the open sky and the wild
is frightened by the patrolling cars
is waiting for the visitors to return

parts.answer: (b) he longs for the freedom of the open sky and the wild — the stars are free and far away, beyond the bars he cannot cross.

parts.prompt: Why does the tiger ignore the visitors? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He is angry and helpless in captivity — 'In his quiet rage' — and the visitors are only people who come to look at him on show. Instead of hunting in the wild he paces the length of his cage and shuts them out. (1 mark: his anger/helplessness at being caged; 1 mark: the visitors as a reminder of his captivity.)

questions.extract: TENTH May dawned bright and clear. For the past few days I had been pleasantly besieged by dignitaries and world leaders who were coming to pay their respects before the inauguration. The inauguration would be the largest gathering ever of international leaders on South African soil. The ceremonies took place in the lovely sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria. For decades this had been the seat of white supremacy, and now it was the site of a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations for the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government.

parts.prompt: Mandela says he had been 'pleasantly besieged'. This means he had been

options.text: attacked by an army for several days
troubled by guests he did not want to meet
surrounded by many visitors whose arrival he welcomed
kept away from the ceremony by his guards

parts.answer: (c) — 'besieged' means surrounded closely, and 'pleasantly' shows he was glad of the dignitaries and world leaders coming to pay their respects.

parts.prompt: Where did the inauguration ceremonies take place?
parts.answer: In the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria.

parts.prompt: The phrase 'a rainbow gathering' suggests

options.text: a ceremony held after the rain
people of many races and nations coming together
guests dressed in bright colours
a crowd waving the new flag

parts.answer: (b) — 'a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations': like the colours of a rainbow, many peoples together.

parts.prompt: What change does Mandela point to when he contrasts 'the seat of white supremacy' with 'the site of a rainbow gathering'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: For decades the Union Buildings had been the centre of white rule. Now the same place hosted people of all colours and nations to install South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government — a change from racial domination to equality. (1 mark: what the place had been; 1 mark: what it had become.)

questions.extract:
He stalks in his vivid stripes
The few steps of his cage,
On pads of velvet quiet,
In his quiet rage.

He should be lurking in shadow,
Sliding through long grass
Near the water hole
Where plump deer pass.

parts.prompt: 'The few steps of his cage' suggests that the cage is

options.text: very small for the tiger
built on a flight of steps
open on one side
large enough for him to run in

parts.answer: (a) very small — the tiger can take only a few steps before he must turn.

parts.prompt: Which phrase describes the soft, silent way the tiger walks?
parts.answer: 'On pads of velvet quiet'.

parts.prompt: In the wild, the tiger 'should be lurking in shadow' near the water hole because he would

options.text: be afraid of the deer
be hiding from hunters
want to cool himself in the water
wait there unseen for the plump deer that pass

parts.answer: (d) — he would lie hidden, as a hunter does, 'Near the water hole / Where plump deer pass'.

parts.prompt: Why do you think the poet mentions the tiger's 'vivid stripes' in a cage only a few steps long? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The vivid stripes show the tiger's beauty and wild splendour. Set against a cage of a few steps, they may suggest that this magnificent animal is wasted and out of place in captivity. Accept other well-argued readings. (1 mark: what the stripes show; 1 mark: the contrast with the cage.)

questions.stem: What 'twin obligations' does Mandela speak of, and why could a man of his birth and colour not fulfil both in South Africa? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Obligations to his family — his parents, wife and children.
Obligations to his people, his community and his country.
In South Africa a man of colour who tried to live as a human being was punished and isolated.
A man who served his people was 'ripped from his family and his home' and forced into 'a twilight existence of secrecy and rebellion'.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Names both obligations and explains why apartheid made it impossible to fulfil both.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: How did Mandela's understanding of freedom change from his boyhood to the day he joined the African National Congress? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: As a boy he felt born free — to run in the fields, swim in the stream, roast mealies and ride bulls.
As a student he wanted 'transitory freedoms' for himself: staying out at night, reading what he pleased, going where he chose.
As a young man in Johannesburg he yearned for basic, honourable freedoms: achieving his potential, earning his keep, marrying and having a family.
When he saw that his brothers and sisters were not free, his hunger for his own freedom became the greater hunger for the freedom of his people, and he joined the ANC.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Traces the stages from personal freedom to the freedom of his people, with at least one detail from the text.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Describe how the two national anthems were sung at the inauguration, and explain what this scene symbolised for Mandela. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' and blacks sang 'Die Stem', the old anthem of the Republic.
Neither group knew the lyrics of the anthem they once despised, but 'they would soon know the words by heart'.
For Mandela the day was symbolised by this scene: the races honouring each other's anthem showed a new, united, non-racial South Africa.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Who sang which anthem, and what the scene stood for.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: How does Leslie Norris contrast the tiger in the zoo with the tiger in the wild in 'A Tiger in the Zoo'? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: In the zoo he stalks 'the few steps of his cage' in 'quiet rage', locked in a concrete cell with his strength behind bars.
In the wild he would be 'lurking in shadow, / Sliding through long grass / Near the water hole / Where plump deer pass'.
He would be snarling around houses at the jungle's edge, baring his fangs and claws, terrorising the village.
The contrast shows a powerful, free predator reduced to a helpless, angry captive.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: At least one detail of the caged tiger and one of the wild tiger, with the point of the contrast.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: What does Mandela mean when he says 'Freedom is indivisible'? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: Freedom cannot be divided between some people and others: 'the chains on anyone of my people were the chains on all of them'.
'The chains on all of my people were the chains on me' — he was not free while they were not.
He could not enjoy 'the poor and limited freedoms' he was allowed when he knew his people were not free.
So his personal struggle became the struggle for the freedom of all his people.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Explains that one person's lack of freedom is everyone's, with a supporting detail from the text.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: In 'A Tiger in the Zoo', the poet repeats words in 'On pads of velvet quiet, / In his quiet rage' and 'stares with his brilliant eyes / At the brilliant stars'. What is the effect of this repetition? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: The first 'quiet' describes his soft, silent tread; the second shows his anger held in, helpless.
The repetition of 'quiet' sets his graceful power against his suppressed rage.
'Brilliant eyes' and 'brilliant stars' link the tiger to the free, distant sky.
It may suggest his longing for the freedom he has lost; it also adds rhythm and emphasis.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Explains the effect of both repetitions, or one in depth, with reference to the tiger's situation.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

valuePoints: Speech format: greeting the audience, stating the topic, a closing thank-you.

Arguments for zoos: protecting or conserving some species, and educating the public.
Arguments against, or alternatives: confinement and loss of natural life; wildlife sanctuaries and national parks.
A clear, reasoned personal conclusion.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Uses the poem and weighs arguments on both sides to reach a reasoned view.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Speech format (address, opening, conclusion); ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

A new student in your class is being teased for the colour of their skin and the way they speak. Write an article for your school magazine, in about 100–120 words, titled 'Taught to Love', drawing on Mandela's words and suggesting how students can make every classmate feel respected.
valuePoints: Article format: title, and an opening that sets out the problem.
Mandela's idea that no one is born hating, and that love comes more naturally to the human heart.
How teasing someone for their colour or background hurts them — imagining how it feels.
Practical steps: speaking up, including the new student, talking to a teacher.
A reasoned conclusion.

rubric.descriptor: Uses Mandela's words and extends them to real, respectful ways of treating a classmate.

Mandela's idea that the oppressor is 'locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrowmindedness'.
Examples of discrimination today — by colour, religion, gender, background — and what it does to both sides.
Counter-arguments considered and answered.
A reasoned conclusion.

questions.stem: The young seagull stood on one leg on the brink of the ledge, closed one eye, then the other, 'and pretended to be falling asleep'. Why did he do this?

options.text: He was exhausted after trying to fly all morning.
He wanted his family to leave the plateau.
He was trying to draw his family's attention, since nobody had come near him.
He was copying the way his father rested.

questions.explanation: Nobody had come near him for twenty-four hours, and he was hungry. The next sentence — 'Still they took no notice of him' — shows that the pretence was meant to make his family notice him.

questions.stem: In 'The Black Aeroplane', why is the woman's reply at the control centre the most important moment of the story?

options.text: It suggests that the aeroplane which guided the narrator may not have been a real aeroplane at all.
It proves that the narrator's radio had been working all along.
It shows that the narrator had landed at the wrong airport.
It reveals that the black aeroplane crashed in the storm.

questions.explanation: She says, 'No other aeroplanes were flying tonight. Yours was the only one I could see on the radar.' The narrator is left asking who the pilot 'on the strange black aeroplane, flying in the storm, without lights' was — the mystery the story ends on.

questions.stem: Much of the humour of 'How to Tell Wild Animals' comes from the fact that each 'rule' for identifying an animal

options.text: is taken from a scientific guide to wildlife
warns the reader never to enter a jungle
depends only on the colour of the animal
works only after the animal has attacked, when it is too late

questions.explanation: You will know the lion 'as you're dyin'', the Bengal Tiger if you 'notice if he eats you', and the Leopard 'As soon as he has lept on you'. The identification comes at the moment it is useless, which is the joke.

questions.stem: When his mother screamed back derisively, the young seagull 'kept calling plaintively'. What does 'plaintively' tell us about his calls?

options.text: They were loud and angry.
They were sad and pleading.
They were proud and joyful.
They were mocking and rude.

questions.explanation: He was hungry and 'begging her to bring him some food', so his calls were mournful and pleading. His scream becomes 'joyful' only after his mother picks up a piece of fish.

questions.stem: After landing, the narrator of 'The Black Aeroplane' says, 'I landed and was not sorry to walk away from the old Dakota.' What does this most likely show?

options.text: He was angry that the Dakota was old and slow.
He wanted to fly a different aeroplane the next day.
He had been told to leave the aeroplane at once.
He was relieved to be safe after a frightening, dangerous flight.

questions.explanation: He had flown with a dead compass, a dead radio and fuel for only 'five or ten minutes more', and was 'starting to feel frightened again'. Walking away from the aeroplane shows relief at having survived.

questions.extract: But when she was just opposite to him, she halted, her wings motionless, the piece of fish in her beak almost within reach of his beak. He waited a moment in surprise, wondering why she did not come nearer, and then, maddened by hunger, he dived at the fish. With a loud scream he fell outwards and downwards into space. Then a monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still. He could hear nothing. But it only lasted a minute. The next moment he felt his wings spread outwards.

parts.prompt: What made the young seagull dive at the fish?

options.text: His father's command
Hunger that drove him beyond his fear
A strong gust of wind
His brothers' taunting

parts.answer: (b) hunger — 'maddened by hunger, he dived at the fish.'

parts.prompt: Which phrase in the extract shows how extreme the seagull's fear was as he fell?
parts.answer: 'a monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still'.

parts.prompt: In 'But it only lasted a minute', the word 'it' refers to

options.text: the piece of fish
the mother's flight across
the seagull's terror as he fell
the family's screaming

parts.answer: (c) the seagull's terror as he fell — the next moment his wings spread and he was no longer afraid.

parts.prompt: Why do you think the mother halted just out of the young seagull's reach? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Scolding and threats had not made him fly, so she used his hunger. Stopping just out of reach made him dive at the fish, and once he fell off the ledge his wings spread and he flew. (1 mark: a deliberate way to make him leave the ledge; 1 mark: the result.)

questions.extract:
What is the boy now, who has lost his ball,
What, what is he to do? I saw it go
Merrily bouncing, down the street, and then
Merrily over — there it is in the water!
No use to say ‘O there are other balls’:
An ultimate shaking grief fixes the boy
As he stands rigid, trembling, staring down
All his young days into the harbour where
His ball went. I would not intrude on him;

parts.prompt: The poet says it is 'No use to say "O there are other balls"' because

options.text: the boy's grief is about more than a ball that can be replaced
no other balls can be bought in the town
the boy refuses to play with new balls
the poet has no money to offer the boy

parts.answer: (a) the boy's grief is about more than a replaceable ball — he is feeling loss itself, and the ball carried his young days.

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract means that the boy stands stiff and unmoving?
parts.answer: Rigid.

parts.prompt: 'staring down / All his young days into the harbour' suggests that

options.text: the boy has lived beside the harbour all his life
the boy is afraid of deep water
the boy is planning to swim after the ball
the ball held memories of the days of his childhood

parts.answer: (d) the ball held memories of his childhood — with it, he watches those days disappear into the water.

parts.prompt: Why does the poet decide not to intrude on the boy? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The boy must learn for himself what loss means and 'how to stand up' after it. Comfort or money for another ball would not help, since 'A dime, another ball, is worthless' and 'no one buys a ball back'. (1 mark: he must learn it alone; 1 mark: money or a replacement cannot help.)

questions.extract: Then, in the black clouds quite near me, I saw another aeroplane. It had no lights on its wings, but I could see it flying next to me through the storm. I could see the pilot's face -- turned towards me. I was very glad to see another person. He lifted one hand and waved. "Follow me," he was saying. "Follow me." ‘He knows that I am lost,’ I thought. ‘He's trying to help me.’ He turned his aeroplane slowly to the north, in front of my Dakota, so that it would be easier for me to follow him. I was very happy to go behind the strange aeroplane like an obedient child.

parts.prompt: The narrator was 'very glad to see another person' because he

options.text: had not seen anyone since leaving Paris
was lost in the storm with no radio or compass
wanted company for his breakfast
recognised the pilot as a friend

parts.answer: (b) — the compass, instruments and radio were dead, and 'I was lost in the storm.'

parts.prompt: Which detail in the extract makes the other aeroplane seem strange?
parts.answer: It had no lights on its wings (yet it could be seen flying through the storm).

parts.prompt: 'like an obedient child' shows that the narrator

options.text: was too young to fly an aeroplane
felt ashamed of getting lost
followed the other pilot trustingly, without question
was being scolded by the other pilot

parts.answer: (c) — he went behind the strange aeroplane trustingly, as a child follows a parent.

parts.prompt: How did the other pilot guide the narrator without speaking to him over the radio? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: He turned his face towards the narrator, lifted one hand and waved, as if saying 'Follow me'. Then he turned slowly to the north in front of the Dakota so that it would be easier to follow him. (1 mark: the gesture; 1 mark: flying slowly ahead to lead.)

questions.extract:
He senses first responsibility
In a world of possessions. People will take
Balls, balls will be lost always, little boy.
And no one buys a ball back. Money is external.
He is learning, well behind his desperate eyes,
The epistemology of loss, how to stand up
Knowing what every man must one day know
And most know many days, how to stand up.

parts.prompt: 'He senses first responsibility / In a world of possessions' suggests that the boy is beginning to realise that

options.text: he must now buy his own toys
things we own can be lost, and we must learn to bear their loss
possessions matter more than people
someone else is to blame for losing the ball

parts.answer: (b) — in a world where 'balls will be lost always', owning things brings the responsibility of accepting their loss.

parts.prompt: Which word in the extract shows that the boy feels hopeless?
parts.answer: 'desperate' (in 'his desperate eyes').

parts.prompt: 'Money is external' means that money

options.text: is kept outside the home
must be earned by working outside
cannot reach or repair the inner feeling of loss
is more important than the ball

parts.answer: (c) — money can buy another ball but cannot touch what the boy feels inside; 'no one buys a ball back'.

parts.prompt: Why is 'how to stand up' repeated, and what do the words 'most know many days' suggest? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The repetition stresses the real lesson: to recover and carry on after a loss. 'Most know many days' suggests that loss is not a single event — most people face it again and again in life. (1 mark: the repetition; 1 mark: 'most know many days'.)

questions.extract:
If when you're walking round your yard
You meet a creature there,
Who hugs you very, very hard,
Be sure it is a Bear.
If you have any doubts, I guess
He'll give you just one more caress.

parts.prompt: According to the stanza, you may 'Be sure it is a Bear' when the creature

options.text: roars at you loudly
has spots on its hide
smiles at you merrily
hugs you very, very hard

parts.answer: (d) it hugs you very, very hard.

parts.prompt: Which word in the stanza means 'a gentle, loving touch'?
parts.answer: Caress.

parts.prompt: The humour of 'He'll give you just one more caress' lies in

options.text: the bear being a pet kept in the yard
a crushing, dangerous hug being called a gentle, loving touch
the reader wanting the bear to hug them again
the bear apologising for hugging too hard

parts.answer: (b) — a hard, harmful squeeze is called a 'caress', a gentle and loving touch.

parts.prompt: What is funny about the poet's advice 'If you have any doubts'? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Instead of a safe way to settle your doubt, the poet says the bear will simply hug you again. You can only be sure by being squeezed a second time, so the 'help' is useless and dangerous. (1 mark: what the advice says; 1 mark: why it is absurd/funny.)

questions.extract:
The true Chameleon is small,
A lizard sort of thing;
He hasn't any ears at all,
And not a single wing.
If there is nothing on the tree,
'Tis the chameleon you see.

parts.prompt: In this stanza the chameleon is described as

options.text: a large and tawny beast
a bird with bright feathers
a small lizard-like creature with no ears or wings
a fierce animal that attacks from trees

parts.answer: (c) — 'small, / A lizard sort of thing; / He hasn't any ears at all, / And not a single wing.'

parts.prompt: Which phrase shows that the poet describes the chameleon in a casual, unscientific way?
parts.answer: 'A lizard sort of thing'.

parts.prompt: 'If there is nothing on the tree, / 'Tis the chameleon you see.' The joke depends on the chameleon's ability to

options.text: blend into its surroundings so that it cannot be seen
fly from tree to tree
hear sounds without ears
grow very large in a moment

parts.answer: (a) — a chameleon matches its surroundings, so seeing 'nothing' on the tree is, jokingly, how you 'see' it.

parts.prompt: How is this last stanza different from the earlier stanzas about the lion, tiger, leopard and bear? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The earlier animals are large, dangerous beasts, identified only when they attack you. The chameleon is small and harmless, and you 'identify' it by seeing nothing at all — a gentler, puzzling joke to end the poem. (1 mark: the kind of animal; 1 mark: the different way of 'telling' it.)

questions.stem: Why was the young seagull afraid to fly, and how did his family try to make him fly? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: The great expanse of sea stretched far below — 'miles down' — and he felt certain his wings would never support him.
His parents called to him shrilly, scolded him and threatened to let him starve on the ledge unless he flew.
His family walked about on the plateau taunting him with his cowardice.
Finally his mother used food: she flew towards him with a piece of fish and halted just out of reach.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The reason for his fear and at least two ways the family tried to push him.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Why did the narrator of 'The Black Aeroplane' fly into the storm, and what happened to him inside the clouds? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: He could not fly over the huge storm clouds and did not have enough fuel to fly around them.
He knew he ought to go back to Paris, but he wanted to get home and have his English breakfast: 'I'll take the risk.'
Inside the clouds everything was black and the aeroplane jumped and twisted.
The compass, the other instruments and the radio were dead; he was lost in the storm.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Why he took the risk and what went wrong inside the storm.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: What do the words 'upbraiding', 'taunting' and 'derisively' tell us about the way the young seagull's family treated him before his first flight? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: 'Upbraiding' means scolding: his parents scolded him and threatened to let him starve.
'Taunting' shows the family mocking his cowardice as they walked about on the plateau.
'Derisively' describes his mother screaming 'Gaw-col-ah' back at him in a mocking way when he begged for food.
Together the words show harsh, pushing treatment meant to force him to fly.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: The meaning of the words in context and what they show about the family's treatment of him.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: In 'How to Tell Wild Animals', the poet takes liberties with language in words such as 'dyin'', 'lept' and in the line 'A novice might nonplus'. Why does she do this? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: 'dyin'' is shortened so that it rhymes with 'lion'.
'lept' and 'lep' are spelt the way they sound, keeping the rhythm and adding to the fun.
'A novice might nonplus' should correctly be 'A novice might be nonplussed'; the poet's version keeps the metre and rhymes with 'thus'.
These liberties add to the humour of the poem.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Explains at least two of the liberties and the reason (rhyme, rhythm, humour).

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: How did the young seagull's family behave once he had flown, and what does this suggest about their earlier harshness? Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: His mother swooped past him calling, and his father flew over him screaming.
His brothers and sister flew around him, curveting, banking, soaring and diving.
When he floated on the sea they surrounded him, praising him and offering him scraps of dog-fish.
This suggests their scolding and taunting had been meant to push him to fly, not to hurt him.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: At least two details of the family's response and a reasoned link to their earlier harshness.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Who do you think helped the narrator of 'The Black Aeroplane' to land safely? Give reasons from the story for your answer. Answer in 40–50 words.
valuePoints: The black aeroplane had no lights, yet the narrator could see it and the pilot's face in the storm.
When he came out of the clouds, the sky was empty and the aeroplane was gone.
The woman in the control centre said no other aeroplanes were flying and only his was on the radar.
Possible views: a ghostly or unexplained helper, or the narrator's own imagination and instinct guiding him under stress — any well-supported view is accepted.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: A clear view of who or what helped, supported by at least two details from the story.

rubric.label: Expression
rubric.descriptor: Clear, connected sentences in about 40–50 words, with accurate grammar and spelling.

questions.stem: Your younger cousin has been chosen to speak at the school's annual day but is so frightened that they want to withdraw. Like the young seagull on his ledge, they are sure they will fail. Write a letter to your cousin, in about 100–120 words, using the seagull's story to help them face their fear.
valuePoints: Informal letter format: address, date, greeting, closing.
Acknowledges the fear as natural — the seagull too was certain his wings would not support him.
The seagull's fear lasted only a minute; once he leapt, he found he could fly and forgot he had ever been afraid.
Practical advice: practise, take one step at a time, trust the people who believe in you.
Encouraging, warm conclusion.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Uses the seagull's story and turns it into real, encouraging advice for facing fear.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Informal letter format; ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and tone.

questions.stem: The pilot in 'The Black Aeroplane' knew he ought to go back to Paris, but he wanted his breakfast at home, so he said, 'I'll take the risk,' and flew into the storm. Write a paragraph, in about 100–120 words, on 'Taking Risks: Brave or Careless?', judging his decision and explaining how young people can decide when a risk is worth taking.
valuePoints: The pilot's choice: a small reward (getting home for breakfast) weighed against a great danger (a storm, little fuel).
The result: dead instruments, no radio, almost no fuel — he survived only through help he could not explain.
A clear judgement on whether the decision was brave or careless.
Guidance for young people: weigh what could be gained against what could be lost, listen to warnings, consider safer options.
A reasoned conclusion.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Judges the pilot's decision and extends it to sensible guidance on risk-taking.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: A single well-structured paragraph with a topic sentence and conclusion; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and tone.

questions.stem: In 'The Ball Poem', the poet chooses not to intrude on the boy, because he must learn 'how to stand up' after a loss. Your younger brother has lost a gift that meant a great deal to him, and he refuses to talk to anyone. Write a diary entry, in about 100–120 words, describing how you felt watching him and how you decided to support him without taking away the chance to learn from the loss.
valuePoints: Diary format: date, first person, reflective tone.
Your brother's grief, and why the gift mattered more than its price — as the ball held the boy's 'young days'.
The poet's idea that some things cannot be bought back, and that loss has to be understood from within.
A thoughtful choice: giving him space, being there to listen, not rushing to replace what was lost.
A reflection on what you learnt about supporting someone.

rubric.label: Content
rubric.descriptor: Understanding of the brother's feelings, drawing on the poem, and a caring, reasoned way of supporting him.

rubric.label: Organisation
rubric.descriptor: Diary format (date, first person); ideas in a logical order; about 100–120 words.

rubric.label: Accuracy
rubric.descriptor: Grammar, spelling and punctuation; appropriate vocabulary and tone.

questions.stem: Anne recalls the saying, 'Paper has more patience than people.' What does this tell us about why she began her diary?

options.text: She hoped to publish her writing and become famous.
She had no true friend to confide in, and paper would listen without judging.
Her teacher had told the class to keep a daily record.
Her parents had forbidden her to talk at home.

questions.explanation: Anne writes, 'Now I'm back to the point that prompted me to keep a diary in the first place: I don't have a friend.' She wants 'to get all kinds of things off my chest', and a diary is patient in a way people are not.

questions.stem: After Anne's poem about the ducklings, 'Mr Keesing took the joke the right way.' What does this reveal about him?

options.text: He was afraid that Anne would complain to her parents.
He had not understood that the poem was about him.
He could enjoy wit and humour even when the joke was on him.
He had decided to stop teaching Anne's class.

questions.explanation: He read the poem to the class 'adding his own comments, and to several other classes as well', stopped giving her extra homework, and is now 'always making jokes'. He could appreciate cleverness turned against himself.

questions.stem: In 'Amanda!', who speaks the stanzas written in brackets?

options.text: Amanda, imagining herself somewhere free
The adult, remembering her own childhood
The poet, commenting on Amanda's behaviour
Amanda's friend, trying to comfort her

questions.explanation: The bracketed stanzas are in the first person — 'I am an orphan', 'I am Rapunzel' — and describe the calm, free worlds Amanda escapes into while an elder keeps instructing her.

questions.stem: Anne writes that the note about the essay 'caught my eye'. Under which word would you look for this idiomatic expression in a dictionary?

options.text: caught
catch
my
eye

questions.explanation: The chapter explains that you look under the first 'meaningful' word, which here is 'caught'. But 'caught' is the past tense of 'catch', so it is listed under 'catch' — that is where the expression 'caught my eye' is found.

questions.stem: Of her sixth-form teacher, Anne writes, 'At the end of the year we were both in tears as we said a heartbreaking farewell.' What does this suggest?

options.text: Anne and Mrs Kuperus shared a close, affectionate bond.
Anne had been kept back and could not move up.
Mrs Kuperus had punished Anne on the last day.
Anne was afraid of her new headmistress.

questions.explanation: Both teacher and pupil were 'in tears', and Anne calls the farewell 'heartbreaking'. Parting would only be so painful if the two had grown fond of each other.

questions.extract: Let me put it more clearly, since no one will believe that a thirteen-year-old girl is completely alone in the world. And I'm not. I have loving parents and a sixteen-year-old sister, and there are about thirty people I can call friends. I have a family, loving aunts and a good home. No, on the surface I seem to have everything, except my one true friend. All I think about when I'm with friends is having a good time. I can't bring myself to talk about anything but ordinary everyday things.

parts.prompt: 'on the surface I seem to have everything' suggests that Anne

options.text: is proud of her family's wealth
is unhappy with her parents
has too many friends to manage
lacks something deeper that others cannot see

parts.answer: (d) she lacks something deeper — 'except my one true friend'.

parts.prompt: Which phrase in the extract shows that Anne's conversations with her friends stay on the surface?
parts.answer: 'ordinary everyday things' (she cannot bring herself to talk about anything else).

parts.prompt: The expression 'can't bring myself to' means

options.text: am not allowed to
cannot make myself do something
keep forgetting to
refuse to listen to

parts.answer: (b) cannot make myself do something (because it feels too difficult).

parts.prompt: Why does Anne feel alone, although she has loving parents and about thirty friends? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: She has no one true friend to confide in. With friends she only has a good time and talks about ordinary things, so they never get closer; that is why she makes the diary, 'Kitty', her friend. (1 mark: no confidant; 1 mark: friendships stay on the surface.)

questions.extract:
Did you finish your homework, Amanda?
Did you tidy your room, Amanda?
I thought I told you to clean your shoes,
Amanda!

(I am an orphan, roaming the street.
I pattern soft dust with my hushed, bare feet.
The silence is golden, the freedom is sweet.)

parts.prompt: The first stanza of the extract is made up of

options.text: Amanda's own thoughts
a conversation between two friends
an elder's questions and instructions, nagging Amanda
a teacher's praise for Amanda's work

questions.extract: That evening, after I'd finished the rest of my homework, the note about the essay caught my eye. I began thinking about the subject while chewing the tip of my fountain pen. I thought and thought, and suddenly I had an idea. I wrote the three pages Mr Keesing had assigned me and was satisfied. I argued that talking is a student's trait and that I would do my best to keep it under control, but that I would never be able to cure myself of the habit since my mother talked as much as I did if not more, and that there's not much you can do about inherited traits.

talk or write aimlessly for a long time
stop and think carefully

come up with convincing arguments to prove the necessity of talking
apologise to Mr Keesing and promise never to talk again
ask her mother to help her write it

parts.prompt: What qualities of Anne does this extract reveal? Answer in 30–40 words.

questions.stem: At the end of 'The Trees', 'The moon is broken like a mirror, / its pieces flash now in the crown / of the tallest oak.' What has most likely caused this change in how the moon appears?

all the animals had been hunted
nobody visited it at night

Belinda punishes the pets for running away.

questions.stem: The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami for mustard-seed 'from a house where no one has lost a child, husband, parent or friend'. Why did he set this condition instead of simply telling her that death comes to everyone?

options.text: He wanted to keep her busy until her grief faded with time.
He wanted her to discover for herself that death is common to all.
He believed such mustard-seed could really bring her son back to life.
He wanted to test whether her neighbours would be generous to her.

questions.explanation: No such house existed: 'there was no house but some beloved one had died in it.' Searching from house to house, Kisa Gotami realised on her own, 'Death is common to all' — a lesson learnt through her own experience rather than simply being told.

questions.stem: Kisa Gotami thinks, 'yet in this valley of desolation there is a path that leads him to immortality who has surrendered all selfishness.' What does 'this valley of desolation' refer to?

options.text: The city of Benares on the river Ganges
The wayside where she sat down, tired and hopeless
The house where her son had died
The world of mortals, which is full of sorrow and loss

questions.explanation: Desolation means deep sorrow; she has just 'considered the fate of men, that their lives flicker up and are extinguished again'. The 'valley' is the whole world of human life, filled with grief because everyone dies — not any single place.

questions.stem: In 'For Anne Gregory', the old religious man found 'a text to prove / That only God, my dear, / Could love you for yourself alone / And not your yellow hair.' What does this final stanza suggest?

options.text: Human love is almost always drawn by outward beauty; love for the inner self alone is divine.
Religious people do not care about beauty of any kind.
Dyeing her hair would make the young woman loved for herself.
Young men are wrong to feel despair at a woman's beauty.

questions.explanation: The young woman believes changing her hair colour will make men love her 'for myself alone'. The speaker answers that only God can love a person that way — implying that human love is always tied to how a person looks, and that pure love of the inner self is beyond humans.

questions.stem: 'Kisa Gotami repaired to the Buddha and cried, "Lord and Master, give me the medicine that will cure my boy."' In present-day English, 'repaired to' means

options.text: went to
mended something for
prayed to
apologised to

questions.explanation: The book glosses 'repaired' as 'a stylistic use' meaning 'went to'. It has nothing to do with fixing something: Kisa Gotami simply went to the Buddha, as the man had told her to.

questions.stem: The Buddha says that while relatives look on and lament, 'one by one mortals are carried off, like an ox that is led to the slaughter.' What does this comparison stress?

options.text: That people who are strong like oxen live longer than others
That death comes as a punishment for bad deeds
That relatives are to blame for not saving the dying
That mortals are helpless before death, and no one watching can stop it

questions.explanation: An ox led to the slaughter cannot escape its end. The Buddha has just said 'a father cannot save his son, nor kinsmen their relations', so the image stresses that death takes each person in turn and weeping relatives are powerless to prevent it.

questions.extract:
Kisa Gotami had an only son, and he died. In her grief she carried the dead child to all her neighbours, asking them for medicine, and the people said, "She has lost her senses. The boy is dead."
At length, Kisa Gotami met a man who replied to her request, "I cannot give thee medicine for thy child, but I know a physician who can."
And the girl said, "Pray tell me, sir; who is it?" And the man replied, "Go to Sakyamuni, the Buddha."

parts.prompt: The people said Kisa Gotami had 'lost her senses' because she

options.text: had stopped speaking to her neighbours
was wandering far from her own home
was asking for medicine for a child who was already dead
refused to accept any help that was offered

parts.answer: (c) — she carried the dead child around 'asking them for medicine', though 'The boy is dead.'

parts.prompt: Rewrite in present-day English: 'I cannot give thee medicine for thy child.'
parts.answer: I cannot give you medicine for your child. ('thee' = you; 'thy' = your.)

parts.prompt: The phrase 'Pray tell me', as used in the extract, is

options.text: a polite, old-fashioned way of saying 'Please tell me'
a request to say a prayer for her son
an angry demand for an answer
a question about whether the man is religious

parts.answer: (a) — 'Pray' here is an old-fashioned word for 'please'.

parts.prompt: How did the man who sent Kisa Gotami to the Buddha show more understanding than her other neighbours? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: The neighbours only declared that she had lost her senses. The man did not mock her; he gently said he had no medicine and directed her to someone who could truly help — the Buddha, the 'physician' who could heal her grief. (1 mark: the neighbours' dismissive response; 1 mark: the man's kind, helpful response.)

questions.extract:
"Never shall a young man,
Thrown into despair
By those great honey-coloured
Ramparts at your ear,
Love you for yourself alone
And not your yellow hair."

"But I can get a hair-dye
And set such colour there,
Brown, or black, or carrot,
That young men in despair
May love me for myself alone
And not my yellow hair."

parts.prompt: 'Those great honey-coloured / Ramparts at your ear' refers to the young woman's

options.text: golden earrings
beautiful yellow hair falling beside her ears
proud and unfriendly manner
high-walled family house

parts.answer: (b) — her thick yellow hair, compared to ramparts (the high walls of a fort) around her ears.

parts.prompt: What does the young woman say she can do about her hair?
parts.answer: She can dye it another colour — brown, black or carrot.

parts.prompt: What does the young woman want most, according to the second stanza?

options.text: To look more fashionable than other women
To put an end to the young men's despair
To stop young men from noticing her at all
To be loved for herself and not for her looks

parts.answer: (d) — she wants young men to 'love me for myself alone / And not my yellow hair'.

parts.prompt: Why does the speaker call the hair 'ramparts', and why are young men 'thrown into despair' by it? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: Ramparts are the high protective walls of a fort; her hair is like a barrier that stops young men from seeing and loving the real person inside. They are so overwhelmed by her beauty that they despair of winning her. (1 mark: the rampart image; 1 mark: the reason for despair.)

questions.extract:
Poor Kisa Gotami now went from house to house, and the people pitied her and said, "Here is mustard-seed; take it!" But when she asked, "Did a son or daughter, a father or mother, die in your family?" they answered her, "Alas! the living are few, but the dead are many. Do not remind us of our deepest grief." And there was no house but some beloved one had died in it.
Kisa Gotami became weary and hopeless, and sat down at the wayside watching the lights of the city, as they flickered up and were extinguished again. At last the darkness of the night reigned everywhere.

parts.prompt: The people's words 'the living are few, but the dead are many' mean that

options.text: a disease had recently killed most of the people in the city
over time, far more people have died than are alive, so every family has known loss
they did not want to give away their mustard-seed
they believed Kisa Gotami's son would come back to life

parts.answer: (b) — death has touched every family; 'there was no house but some beloved one had died in it'.

parts.prompt: Rewrite in present-day English: 'there was no house but some beloved one had died in it.'
parts.answer: In every house, someone dear had died. (Accept: There was not a single house where a loved one had not died.)

parts.prompt: The lights of the city that 'flickered up and were extinguished again' most likely suggest

options.text: that the city was running short of oil
that it was time for Kisa Gotami to go home
that human lives, too, begin and then come to an end
that the Buddha was coming to find her

parts.answer: (c) — she 'considered the fate of men, that their lives flicker up and are extinguished again'.

parts.prompt: Why was Kisa Gotami unable to get the mustard-seed, even though everyone was willing to give it? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: People pitied her and offered the seed gladly, but the Buddha wanted it only from a house where no one had lost a child, husband, parent or friend. Every family she asked had lost someone, so no house met the condition. (1 mark: the condition; 1 mark: every house had known a death.)

questions.extract:
"I heard an old religious man

parts.prompt: The word 'yesternight' means

options.text: every night
last night
tomorrow night
many nights ago

parts.answer: (b) last night — an old-fashioned word.

parts.prompt: Whose words does the speaker report in this stanza to support his argument?
parts.answer: An old religious man's, who declared that he had found a text proving that only God could love her for herself alone.

parts.prompt: The lines 'for yourself alone / And not your yellow hair' close every stanza of the poem. This repetition

options.text: shows that the speaker has forgotten what he said earlier
tells us that the young woman has already dyed her hair
suggests that the old religious man agrees with the young woman
keeps the central question of the poem — love for the self or for looks — in focus

parts.answer: (d) — the refrain returns to the one question the two speakers argue about.

parts.prompt: How does this stanza answer the young woman's plan to dye her hair? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: She believed changing her hair colour would make young men love her for herself. The speaker replies that no human love can be separated from looks — only God loves a person for their self alone — so dyeing her hair would not change anything. Weeping does not save the dead; one who draws out the arrow and becomes composed obtains peace of mind.

questions.stem: Natalya says the Oxen Meadows 'aren't worth much to me. They only come to five dessiatins, and are worth perhaps 300 roubles', and Lomov says, 'I don't want the Meadows'. What makes their quarrel comic?

options.text: The Meadows actually belong to the peasants, not to either family.
Lomov is only pretending to be angry in order to impress Natalya.
Both say the land means little to them, yet they fight over it furiously.
Natalya does not know where the Oxen Meadows are.

questions.explanation: Each claims not to care about the land itself — Natalya 'can't stand unfairness', Lomov is 'acting on principle' — yet they shout 'Mine!' and 'Ours!' and threaten mowers and courts. The gap between the petty stake and the fury is the comedy.

questions.stem: During the quarrel, the stage direction reads: '[Quickly steps to the carafe and drinks more water]'. What does this action show about Lomov?

options.text: He is nervous and excitable, and easily upset.
He is calm and in full control of the argument.
He has just returned from a long, hot journey.
He wants to change the subject politely.

questions.explanation: Lomov describes himself as someone who suffers 'from palpitations', 'excitable and always getting awfully upset', and he keeps drinking water whenever he is agitated. The direction shows his nervousness mounting as he is accused of being a landgrabber.

questions.stem: When Lomov arrives, Chubukov says aside, 'He's come to borrow money. Shan't give him any!' Minutes later he says, 'I've always loved you, my angel, as if you were my own son.' What does this contrast reveal?

options.text: Chubukov has always been a generous neighbour to Lomov.
Chubukov is too confused by joy to remember what he thought.
Chubukov had secretly planned the proposal himself.
Chubukov's show of affection is insincere and depends on what he stands to gain.

questions.explanation: His private thought is suspicious and mean; his public warmth appears only once he hears the proposal, which suits his wish to marry off his daughter to a wealthy neighbour. The aside exposes the flattery as self-interest.

questions.stem: LOMOV (to Chubukov): 'I'll prove to you that they're mine!' Which is the correct reported speech?

options.text: Lomov said to Chubukov that I'll prove to you that they're mine.
Lomov declared that he will prove to him that they are his.
Lomov declared to Chubukov that he would prove to him that they were his.
Lomov asked Chubukov if he would prove that they were mine.

questions.explanation: A statement is reported with 'said' or, for a strong claim, 'declared'; 'will' becomes 'would', 'are' becomes 'were', and the pronouns shift: 'I' to 'he', 'you' to 'him', 'mine' to 'his'. The other options keep the direct pronouns or tenses, or turn the statement into a question.

questions.stem: The play ends: 'LOMOV : He's better! NATALYA : Worse! Worse! Worse! CHUBUKOV : [trying to shout her down] Champagne! Champagne!' What does this ending suggest?

options.text: Lomov and Natalya have finally agreed about the dogs.
The engagement is off, and Chubukov is angry.
The couple's quarrelling will go on even after the engagement.
Chubukov has decided that Guess is the better dog.

questions.explanation: Moments after the kiss, Natalya reopens the dispute over Guess and Squeezer and Lomov answers back. Chubukov can only try to drown them out with champagne — as he says, 'that's a way to start your family bliss!' The quarrels are clearly not over.

questions.extract: LOMOV : It's cold... I'm trembling all over, just as if I'd got an examination before me. The great thing is, I must have my mind made up. If I give myself time to think, to hesitate, to talk a lot, to look for an ideal, or for real love, then I'll never get married. Brr... It's cold! Natalya Stepanovna is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking, well-educated. What more do I want? But I'm getting a noise in my ears from excitement. [Drinks] And it's impossible for me not to marry. In the first place, I'm already 35 -- a critical age, so to speak. In the second place, I ought to lead a quiet and regular life.

parts.prompt: Lomov feels he must make up his mind quickly because

options.text: Chubukov has asked him to decide at once
if he stops to think or look for real love, he will never marry
Natalya is about to marry someone else
he has to leave for an examination

parts.prompt: By calling 35 'a critical age', Lomov means that

options.text: his health is in serious danger
he has become very critical of other people
he is getting too old to put off marriage any longer
he is at the best age to buy more land

parts.prompt: What does this speech reveal about Lomov's reasons for marrying? Answer in 30–40 words.
parts.answer: His reasons are practical, not romantic: he wants a good housekeeper, feels he is at 'a critical age', and needs 'a quiet and regular life' for his health. He even says looking for 'real love' would stop him marrying. (1 mark: practical reasons; 1 mark: absence of love, supported from the extract.)
